label: Title
notes: Open with the visual mystery of perspective drawing: parallel railroad tracks appear to converge at a point on the horizon. This chapter explains the mathematics behind that illusion and builds the projective plane, where every pair of lines meets. Orient students to printed pages 88 through 116.

label: Lecture Route
notes: Preview the four themes. Students should leave understanding vanishing points and the geometry of projection, the projective plane as the ordinary plane plus a line at infinity, homogeneous coordinates as the algebraic language of projection, and the cross-ratio as the fundamental invariant of projective geometry.

label: Vanishing Points
notes: Explain vanishing points through the mechanics of perspective projection. When a family of parallel lines is projected onto a picture plane, their images converge at a single vanishing point. Different families of parallels have different vanishing points, and all vanishing points lie on the horizon line.

label: Projective Plane
notes: Present the projective plane as the Euclidean plane augmented by a line at infinity. Each family of parallel lines shares a single point at infinity, and these ideal points form the line at infinity. In this model, every two distinct lines meet in exactly one point.

label: Homogeneous Coordinates
notes: Introduce homogeneous coordinates: a point in the projective plane is represented by a triple of numbers up to scaling. The point at infinity in direction m is represented as the equivalence class of vectors with zero third coordinate.

label: Projections
notes: Present projections and linear fractional maps. A projection from one line to another through a center is described by a linear fractional transformation. These maps preserve the cross-ratio but generally change distances, midpoints, and angles.

label: Cross-Ratio
notes: Define the cross-ratio of four collinear points and show that it is invariant under projection. The formula involves ratios of signed distances between the four points. Since projections change distances but preserve cross-ratios, this is the fundamental measurement tool in projective geometry.

label: Recap
notes: Summarize the chapter by connecting vanishing points, the projective plane, homogeneous coordinates, projections, and the cross-ratio into a unified framework. Projective geometry removes the special status of parallel lines and replaces distance with the cross-ratio as its fundamental invariant.
